title: IB Philosophy Exam Technique for November
summary: IB Philosophy exam technique for November: master Paper 1, Paper 2 and HL Paper 3 with a focused three-week plan, timing tactics and essay tips.
body_markdown:
The final three weeks before the November session can feel strangely philosophical. Time appears to accelerate. Certainty becomes difficult. Even the question, “Have I revised enough?” begins to resemble an unsolved problem in epistemology.


The practical answer is simpler. Strong **IB Philosophy exam technique** means knowing what each paper demands, planning before writing, explaining arguments precisely and evaluating rather than merely describing. In the final weeks, your task is not to learn every possible idea. It is to make your existing knowledge usable under timed conditions.


This guide follows that journey through Paper 1, Paper 2 and, for HL students, Paper 3. The assessment information below follows the current IB Philosophy course structure used for the November session. Always compare it with the timetable and instructions issued by your school, since administrative details can change.


### Your three-week November checklist


Time remaining Main priority Practice target


Three weeks Diagnose gaps and organise arguments One untimed plan for each studied theme and prescribed text


Two weeks Improve analysis and evaluation Timed sections with self-review


Final week Rehearse complete decisions under pressure Full timed papers in Exam mode


A useful routine combines concise[RevisionDojo study resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/) with active recall, argument reconstruction and timed writing. Study Notes can refresh a position, Flashcards can test terminology, and AI Chat can help you interrogate distinctions. None of those replaces writing. Philosophy becomes examinable only when you can turn knowledge into a clear response.


### Three weeks out: understand what each paper rewards


Imagine a student opening a notebook 21 days before the first exam. The pages contain names, quotations and definitions, but few complete arguments. This is common. It is also fixable.


Examiners reward philosophical understanding, relevant argument, analysis, evaluation and coherent organisation. Name-dropping philosophers is not enough. A useful paragraph normally does four things:


- states a focused claim;
- explains the reasoning behind it;
- tests it with an objection, implication or alternative;
- reaches a justified interim judgment.


The pattern is not a rigid formula. It is a safeguard against drifting into description.


### Paper 1: turn knowledge into an argument


Paper 1 lasts 1 hour 45 minutes at SL and 2 hours 30 minutes at HL. SL students answer the core-theme task and one optional-theme essay. HL students answer the core-theme task and two optional-theme essays. The core section is worth 25 marks, while each optional-theme response is worth 25 marks.


This gives SL students roughly 50-55 minutes for each half after allowing planning and checking time. HL students can treat the paper as three blocks of approximately 50 minutes. These are planning guidelines, not IB rules. Adjust them during practice if one task reliably requires more reading.


### Handling the core-theme stimulus


The core theme, *Being human* , begins from stimulus material. The first task asks you to identify and explain a relevant philosophical issue or concept. Start with the issue, not a broad summary of the stimulus.


A strong opening might follow this logic:


1. Identify the philosophical issue precisely.
2. Explain how the stimulus raises it.
3. Define any essential distinction.
4. Develop the consequences or tensions involved.


For the extended discussion, build a contest between defensible positions. Do not treat the image, passage or scenario as something to decode once and abandon. Return to it when it sharpens your analysis, while keeping the philosophical question at the centre.


### Writing the optional-theme essay


Choose the question for which you can construct the best argument, not the one containing the most familiar word. Spend 4-6 minutes planning a thesis, two or three main moves, objections and a conclusion.


Each paragraph should advance the answer. Explain a philosopher’s argument in enough detail for the reasoning to be visible. Then ask whether the premises are credible, whether the conclusion follows and what a rival account explains better. Concrete examples can expose consequences, but examples do not evaluate an argument by themselves.


A student asks a philosopher standing on a giant timer whether time can be defined after the exam


### Two weeks out: master Paper 2 through close reading


Paper 2 lasts 1 hour 15 minutes at both SL and HL and focuses on your prescribed philosophical text. You select one of two questions and write one extended response worth 25 marks.


The danger is preparing a biography of the author or a general summary of the book. Paper 2 rewards a direct response grounded in detailed knowledge of the prescribed text. Your revision should therefore be organised around arguments, concepts, tensions and passages rather than chapters alone.


Create an argument map for each major idea:


- the author’s central claim;
- the premises supporting it;
- a significant concept or distinction;
- a connection to another part of the text;
- one serious objection;
- your reasoned judgment.


In the exam, define the problem posed by the question before presenting your thesis. Refer accurately to the text, but avoid forcing memorised quotations into an argument they do not support. Precise paraphrase is more useful than an impressive quotation with no analysis.


Use the[RevisionDojo Questionbank and study platform](https://www.revisiondojo.com/) to practise selecting questions quickly. After writing, use Grading tools to identify whether your response became descriptive, then revise the weakest paragraph rather than merely reading the feedback.


### HL Paper 3: examine what philosophers are doing


HL students also sit Paper 3, a 1 hour 15 minute response to unseen material worth 25 marks. Its focus is philosophical activity itself, including its nature, purpose and methods.


The unseen passage is a starting point, not a comprehension exercise. Read once for the main position, then annotate claims about how philosophy operates. Look for assumptions about reason, dialogue, evidence, conceptual analysis, lived experience or philosophy’s relationship with culture and other disciplines.


A reliable plan has three stages:


- reconstruct the passage’s view of philosophical activity;
- analyse its assumptions and implications;
- evaluate it through contrasting conceptions, examples and your studied experience of doing philosophy.


Your response should engage with the passage throughout. A pre-written essay about the nature of philosophy will struggle if it barely addresses the author’s claims. Conversely, line-by-line commentary will not provide enough independent evaluation.


### The final week: practise decisions, not just essays


The final week is when **IB Philosophy exam tips** must become habits. Sit complete timed papers in Exam mode. Practise choosing between questions, planning within a fixed limit and moving on when time expires.


Use[RevisionDojo’s IB learning tools](https://www.revisiondojo.com/) as a connected system. Begin with the Questionbank, write under timed conditions, review with Grading tools, and use AI Chat to challenge one weak inference. Predicted Papers and Mock Exams can help recreate the pressure of the session, while the Coursework Library and Tutors can clarify broader philosophical skills without replacing your own judgment.


Keep an error log with three columns: the problem, the cause and the correction. “Weak evaluation” is too vague. “I stated an objection but never judged whether it defeated the premise” tells you what to change.


In the last 24 hours, avoid rebuilding the entire course. Review argument maps, command expectations and timing. Pack what you need, confirm the timetable supplied by your school and sleep.


### A calmer way into the November exams


The best preparation for the **IB Philosophy November exams** is not knowing every possible answer. It is knowing what to do when the exact answer is not waiting in memory.


Read the wording carefully. Define the issue. Reconstruct arguments fairly. Test them seriously. Reach a judgment that follows from your analysis.


That process is philosophy, but it is also exam technique. Practise it in the RevisionDojo Questionbank, then sit timed papers in Exam mode until the structure feels familiar. On the day, the question may still be difficult. The method should not be.
